Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

issues.explanation: For an 18-year-old male whose trauma type is rape, the trigger 'Military Topics' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger, threat, and memory items coherently suggest interpersonal/close-contact danger (touch, strangers, shouting, doors, vivid sensory reliving), but military-related talk implies a trauma context that is otherwise absent. This is not supported by the threat or memory content and does not fit the formulation as a plausible trigger tightly linked to the presented threat-memory pattern.

vignette:
Kofi is an eighteen-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a junior tax consultant at a small accounting firm in Atlanta. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 74, indicating severe posttraumatic stress, and was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure he made to his employee assistance program counselor approximately three weeks ago.

Approximately four months before seeking help, Kofi attended a gathering at the apartment of a colleague he had met shortly after starting his job. He did not know the other people present well. At some point during the evening he was separated from the small group, led into a back room by a man he had trusted enough to follow, and raped. He remembers the sound of the front door slamming shut somewhere in the apartment as it happened - a sound that seemed to seal off any possibility of help arriving. The man had raised his voice at one point, a sharp, commanding shout, and Kofi had gone still. He remembers a specific taste, something metallic and sour, that he cannot fully account for and cannot fully forget.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi told no one. He returned to work, filed spreadsheets, answered emails, and sat in meetings. On the surface very little changed. Beneath it, almost everything did. The memories that returned to him were not narrative - they arrived as images, vivid and fragmentary, a hand, a wall, a shadow across a ceiling. At other times there was no image at all, only an abrupt wave of the same terror and shame he had felt that night, arriving without warning and without context, as though his body had retained the emotional record even when his mind refused to supply the scene. Most disorienting of all, the taste returned. Sitting at his desk eating lunch, or drinking coffee in the break room, that same metallic sourness would appear on his tongue and he would have to set down whatever he was holding and wait for it to pass.

Kofi began to reorganize his life around what he could not yet name. He stopped going anywhere he did not already know well. He had come to believe that in an unfamiliar environment he would have no way of reading the exits, the people, the likelihood of danger, and that belief felt less like anxiety and more like clear-eyed reasoning. When strangers approached him - on the street, in a parking garage, even in the lobby of his own office building - he felt a threat that seemed to him entirely proportionate. He was certain that his body was simply registering information that other people chose to ignore. He stopped taking the elevator when male colleagues were already inside it. He began arriving to the office before anyone else and leaving after most people had gone, a habit that his supervisor initially praised as dedication before noticing that Kofi flinched visibly when a door opened behind him, and that he had begun declining all client-facing assignments that required visiting unfamiliar offices.

That flinch had become a source of private humiliation. An unexpected hand on his shoulder from a well-meaning colleague sent him halfway out of his chair. He began sitting with his back to the wall in the conference room, positioning himself so that no one could approach him from behind. What frightened him most was not that these responses were happening, but that he could not make them stop. He had always thought of himself as composed and capable, someone who had worked hard and arrived early at a professional life most people his age had not yet reached. The gap between that self-image and the person who could not ride an elevator with a man he had known for months felt unbridgeable.

What finally brought him to speak was a performance review. His supervisor noted, gently but in writing, that Kofi had become withdrawn and was limiting his own opportunities. Reading those words, Kofi understood that the life he had been quietly protecting was already contracting around him. He came to his first session hoping, above everything else, to feel safe enough to go back to being who he was before - and terrified, in equal measure, that the person he was before no longer existed.
